title-group.article-title: Continuous quantitative electroencephalography for early detection of acute low-pressure obstructive hydrocephalus in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage: illustrative case

sec.title: BACKGROUND
sec.p: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) is often associated with acute high-pressure hydrocephalus. Less commonly, an acute low-pressure hydrocephalus (ALPH) variant can develop and contribute to increased morbidity. ALPH is particularly challenging to diagnose and manage, as patients present with symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (ICP) despite the absence of corroborating evidence from ICP measurements. Misdiagnosis or delayed recognition can result in increased morbidity.

sec.title: OBSERVATIONS
sec.p: The authors describe a patient with aSAH who developed neurological deterioration from ALPH. Despite normal ICP readings, the patient displayed symptoms of increased ICP. Significant electroencephalography (EEG) changes preceded the neurological deterioration by many hours. In addition, these EEG changes reversed with cerebrospinal fluid removal and eventual hydrocephalus resolution.

sec.title: LESSONS
sec.p: ALPH presents with paradoxical ICP dynamics, complicating its diagnosis. Careful monitoring, including EEG, can provide an early indication of neurological deterioration and guide timely intervention. This case underscores the importance of considering ALPH in patients with aSAH who show clinical worsening without corresponding increases in ICP. Tailoring management to address the atypical pressure dynamics is crucial for improving outcomes.
Keywords: subarachnoid hemorrhage, acute low-pressure hydrocephalus, quantitative electroencephalography, case report

body.p: Acute symptomatic hydrocephalus often occurs as a consequence of aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH).1 While many patients with aSAH-related hydrocephalus develop the typical high-pressure variant with associated intracranial hypertension, a less common form known as “acute low-pressure hydrocephalus” (ALPH), where clinical symptoms and ventricular enlargement occur in the absence of elevated intracranial pressure (ICP), can also occur.2–4 Because ICP remains low in ALPH, the diagnosis can be delayed and management is challenging. Electroencephalography (EEG) abnormalities, especially focal or generalized increases in delta frequency activity, can occur during hydrocephalus.5, 6 However, although EEG has emerged as an important tool for the identification and management of both seizures and delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) after aSAH,1 its use in acute hydrocephalus management is limited and rare. Here, we present the case of a patient with aSAH-induced ALPH, in whom notable changes in quantitative EEG (qEEG) trends preceded clinical deterioration by many hours. Aggressive cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) drainage induced clinical improvement and partially reversed the EEG findings.

sec.title: Illustrative Case
sec.p: A 74-year-old male with an unknown past medical history presented with the sudden onset of vomiting and unresponsiveness. Initial examination demonstrated a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 4 with bilaterally pinpoint pupils, and a noncontrast head computed tomography (NCCT) revealed diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) with hydrocephalus. Computed tomography angiography (CTA) demonstrated a dysplastic aneurysm located in the left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). He was transferred to our institution for further management, and upon arrival, he was noted to have unequal pupils with a GCS score of 3. After administering hyperosmolar therapy, we placed an external ventricular drain (EVD) for CSF drainage. The CSF pressure upon EVD placement was noted to be low at 0 mm Hg. Parasagittal subgaleal EEG electrodes were inserted bilaterally (Fig. 1) to monitor for DCI. Subgaleal EEG data were processed using standard methods for qEEG analysis and integrated with time-locked concurrent hemodynamic and ICP data for real-time and retrospective visualization (iCE Neurosystems). Concurrent surface EEG for seizure monitoring (Natus Medical), utilizing the international 10–20 system, was also initiated soon after admission.

caption.p: Digital subtraction angiography scout images. Anterolateral (A) and lateral (B) views obtained during aneurysm embolization on PBD 1. Blue arrows indicate the position of the subgaleal electrodes.

sec.title: Clinical Course
sec.p: On postbleed day 1 (PBD 1), the patient underwent uncomplicated cerebral angiography, and the distal PICA aneurysm was occluded with Onyx-18 (Medtronic). On PBD 2, the EVD level was lowered from 15 to 0 mm Hg to promote CSF drainage due to persistent unresponsiveness and radiographic evidence of persistent hydrocephalus. Following this intervention, he developed briskly reactive pupils, started following commands, and was able to move all extremities against gravity (GCS score 10). NCCT performed on PBD 2 demonstrated a new hypoattenuation in the left cerebellum in the PICA distribution, consistent with a procedure-related infarct.

From PBD 2 through PBD 4, the neurological examination remained unchanged. However, NCCT performed on PBD 3 demonstrated small bilateral subdural hygromas (Fig. 2A and B). These hygromas were attributed to excessive CSF drainage; therefore, the EVD level was raised on PBD 4 to 10 mm Hg (Fig. 3, point 1). Decreased CSF output (from 172 to 51 mL/day), a modest but clinically insignificant increase in ICP, and a sustained increase in delta power with a concurrent reduction in the alpha/delta ratio (ADR) on qEEG trends occurred in concert with the EVD level increase without any associated clinical change (Fig. 3B, between points 2 and 3). The increased delta power was not related to sedation, as the dexmedetomidine infusion was discontinued on the morning of PBD 4, nor were there any transcranial Doppler (TCD) findings indicative of vasospasm. On PBD 5, almost 24 hours after initially observing the qEEG changes associated with the EVD level increase, the patient stopped following commands (Fig. 3A, point 3). Urgent NCCT demonstrated worsening hydrocephalus (Fig. 2C and D). Approximately 30 mL of CSF was manually drained, and the EVD level was lowered back to 0 mm Hg. Following the increased CSF drainage, the neurological examination improved; however, the delta power remained elevated for another 24 hours (Fig. 3A, between points 3 and 4), finally declining, though not to baseline levels (Fig. 3A, point 4; ), only after sustained increases in CSF output (Fig. 3B, between points 3 and 4). On PBD 7, the EVD level was again raised to 10 mm Hg (Fig. 3B, point 4), and CSF output abruptly declined (Fig. 3B, between points 4 and 5). Although the neurological examination remained unchanged (GCS score 10), qEEG trends during this time period showed fluctuations in delta power that inversely correlated with CSF drainage. Specifically, delta power increased with diminished CSF output and decreased in response to enhanced CSF output, as illustrated in Fig. 3A (highlighted by arrows between points 4 and 5). By PBD 8, as shown in Fig. 3 point 5, the patient’s GCS score improved to 14, and delta power levels declined. ICP remained below 10 mm Hg throughout this observation period, and NCCT indicated a reduction in hydrocephalus with no evidence of new infarcts (Fig. 2E and F). In addition, as part of the DCI risk assessment, CTA and computed tomography perfusion (CTP) studies failed to identify areas of vasospasm or hypoperfusion, respectively. No electrographic seizures were noted on surface EEG, and TCD velocities remained consistently normal throughout the entire period. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) on PBD 10 redemonstrated the procedure-related left cerebellar stroke in the PICA distribution, but hydrocephalus had resolved, and there were no DCI-related infarcts. The EVD was removed, and the remainder of the patient’s clinical course was uneventful. He was later discharged to an acute rehabilitation facility.

sec.p: The necessary informed consent was obtained in this study.

sec.title: Observations
sec.p: We present a case of ALPH where qEEG changes preceded clinical deterioration by many hours. Our findings, which have not been previously reported, support the potential use of qEEG to identify optimal CSF drainage levels in difficult-to-manage ALPH cases in which ICP control cannot be used as a proxy for effective hydrocephalus treatment and to extend the use of EEG monitoring beyond its previously described roles in seizure and DCI management.1 The availability of a continuous bedside graphical display of qEEG can allow clinical staff without specialized training to identify clinically important trends sooner than relying on daily or twice-daily EEG interpretation by an epileptologist. This could allow for more rapid diagnosis and treatment of clinically significant neurological events.

While acute hydrocephalus following aSAH typically results in elevated ICP and can lead to an altered level of consciousness, coma, and death if left untreated,7 the less commonly described low-pressure form of ALPH can lead to prolonged hospitalization and a high rate of morbidity.3, 8 The pathophysiology of ALPH remains unclear, although some have postulated that excess tissue compliance from low brain turgor facilitates ventricular enlargement with corresponding compression of adjacent white matter.9 This white matter insult can impact corticothalamic networks or possibly induce cerebral hypoperfusion, as has been described in chronic normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH).10 Regardless of the mechanism, as seen in our case, the neurological examination typically improves with large-volume CSF removal, which may require subatmospheric drainage or manual hourly drainage of CSF.3

Beyond its established role in detecting DCI and monitoring seizures, qEEG could serve as a valuable tool for monitoring the neurological impacts of acute hydrocephalus. Small case series have noted that increases in EEG delta power can be seen either preceding or during episodes of elevated ICP or neurological deterioration attributed to intracranial hypertension.11, 12 In patients with NPH, a reduction in qEEG delta power following CSF removal was associated with an improved neurological examination.13 However, there is little literature describing qEEG changes associated with ALPH. In this case, we noted a gradual rise in delta power starting many hours prior to neurological examination deterioration and normal ICP, except for a brief initial increase. The elevated delta power persisted until adequate, sustained CSF outflow was achieved, with a concomitant reduction of hydrocephalus on brain imaging, at which point the neurological examination improved to baseline.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: The qEEG is based on subgaleal EEG, which provides limited parasagittal coverage of the brain, and thus may miss focal areas of brain injury; however, with hydrocephalus, the changes tend to be global. While the qEEG and neurological examination changes noted in this patient could be attributed to fever, sedation, or DCI, we believe that this is unlikely for several reasons. First, although this patient’s fever was transient, the delta power changes persisted. Second, sedatives were discontinued prior to the qEEG changes. Third, TCD velocities remained normal, while CTA and CTP demonstrated no vasospasm or hypoperfusion. Fourth, the patient had no DCI-related infarcts on MRI. Finally, the time-locked correlations between delta power, CSF outflow, and ventricular size argue strongly that changes in delta power reflected fluctuations in the degree of hydrocephalus.

sec.title: Lessons
sec.p: This case suggests that increased EEG delta power could be a surrogate for ongoing hydrocephalus, regardless of ICP, particularly if the neurological examination remains abnormal with no clear alternative explanation. Our findings also suggest that interpreting delta power changes in SAH as solely attributable to changes in perfusion secondary to DCI should be done with caution.
